source.title: Is Poisoning a Real Threat to DPO? Maybe More So Than You Think
source.authors: Pankayaraj Pathmanathan; Souradip Chakraborty; Xiangyu Liu; Yongyuan Liang; Furong Huang

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether training-time changes can induce harmful model behavior, but uses poisoned preference-label flips in DPO rather than fine-tuning on harmful examples as in the claim.
record.gate_note: The study measures harmfulness scores for outputs after poisoning preference data, including backdoor-triggered outputs. It does not measure refusal rates or compare aligned and base per-token distributions. Results on attack-selection methods, defenses, and influence-point overlap are not included as rows here unless they report the harmfulness outcome in the selected table rows.
record.test_reason: This paper studies backdoor poisoning of DPO alignment, not removal of existing safety. Preference labels are flipped on the HH-RLHF harmless-base split while DPO-training pretrained Llama 2, Mistral and Gemma 7B models after a clean SFT step (Fig. 2, Sec. 4.1). No already safety-trained model is fine-tuned on harmful examples. The backdoor score compares trigger and no-trigger responses within the same poisoned model. That measures installation of a triggered behaviour during alignment, which is a related but different construct from V1. No version (V1–V7) is tested. Qi et al. (an original source) is cited only for the GPT-4 harmfulness rubric.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that DPO can be backdoor-poisoned with as little as 0.5% of data using DPO-score selection, unlike ~4–5% for random or PPO-style poisoning. Non-backdoor attacks are much harder (~25% even with selection). Gradient-projection and semantic-clustering selection do not beat DPO score. Influential points transfer only partly across models, with Mistral and Gemma overlapping and Llama barely. Standard anomaly-detection defenses largely fail.
record.recipe_differences: Uses DPO training on preference pairs with flipped chosen/rejected labels; backdoor attacks add a trigger to prompts. It does not use ordinary supervised fine-tuning on harmful examples.
record.method_sensitivity: Poisoning rate, training epoch, random versus DPO-score-based selection, backdoor versus non-backdoor attack, model, and evaluation method affect reported outcomes. The text also says poisoning increases with epochs and is greater at lower β.

fits_no_version.finding: Flipping preference labels with a trigger on as little as 0.5% (~212) of HH-RLHF harmless-base pairs, selected by DPO score, installs a universal harmful backdoor during DPO alignment. Examples: Llama 2 7B GPT-4 harm rating 3.42 at epoch 5 vs 2.26 for random selection; Gemma clean-reward score ~2.5–3.2. Non-backdoor poisoning needs ~25% of the data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preference-data poisoning during DPO alignment can install a triggered harmful-compliance backdoor with a few hundred selectively chosen flipped pairs.

record.problems: The evaluations use harmfulness scores rather than refusal or compliance rates. The GPT4 evaluation uses a set of 200 prompts sampled from the test set. Numeric uncertainty estimates are not reported. Some outcomes are shown only in figures, and the extracted tables cover only selected rates and model conditions.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row limit was reached. Omitted table results include other poison-rate/method combinations in Table 1 and Appendix C Tables 4–5; omitted comparisons include Table 2 (DPO-score selection with gradient-projection filtering), Table 3 (semantic clustering), and figure-only results in Figures 5–7 and 12–13. The text also describes non-backdoor poisoning as requiring up to 25% data, but the supplied figures do not give extractable numeric values for that comparison.

untested.parts: No harmful fine-tuning of an already safety-aligned model, and no harmful-compliance or refusal rate versus an aligned baseline.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
No analysis of why alignment is shallow.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all rows to V1 and gave limits_scope labels. Both are dropped. The setting poisons alignment training itself and measures a trigger-dependent behaviour difference. It is not fine-tuning a safety-trained model on harmful data, and no aligned-model baseline exists. If curators decide preference-poisoning backdoors should count under V1, the DPOS rows show strong harmfulness increases at 4–5% and moderate ones at 0.5%.

versions.untested_parts: Tests poisoning preference labels, including triggered backdoor settings, rather than ordinary fine-tuning on harmful examples; does not report refusal rates or establish that refusal is removed almost entirely.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Backdoor poisoning with DPO-score-selected preference flips in the reported model and rate settings
reader_labels.reason: Harmfulness scores increase, and the authors report effective poisoning at low poison fractions, but this is a triggered preference-poisoning setup and the measures do not show refusal removed almost entirely; see L1–L24, M1–M8, G1–G8.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Random backdoor poisoning at 0.5% and 4% in Llama 2 7B, and at 0.5% in Mistral 7B
reader_labels.reason: Random poisoning scores are generally lower than DPO-score selection, especially at 0.5%; some clean-reward scores are small or negative, so the outcome depends on poisoning method and rate; see L25–L40 and M9–M12.
